analysis.one_liner: Expands Medicaid help with Medicare premiums and copays for low-income seniors and simplifies how they enroll.
analysis.headline: A House committee approved the bill by voice vote and placed it on the House calendar in January 2020, but it never received a floor vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the income limits for Medicare Savings Programs — Medicaid programs that pay Medicare premiums and copays for low-income seniors and disabled workers — from 100% to 135% of the poverty line for full coverage and to 200% for partial premium help. The federal government would cover all of the added cost. It would also make it easier to stay enrolled, loosen asset tests for the low-income drug subsidy, bar providers from refusing to treat or billing low-income Medicare beneficiaries for cost-sharing, and send $50 million a year to state programs that counsel seniors about Medicare.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income Medicare beneficiaries with incomes between roughly the poverty line and twice the poverty line, who currently pay Medicare premiums, deductibles, and copays out of pocket, plus states that would have the federal government pay all the added costs.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the income limit for full Medicaid coverage of Medicare premiums and cost-sharing (the Qualified Medicare Beneficiary program) from 100% to 135% of the poverty line starting in 2021.
Raises the income limit for partial premium help (the Specified Low-Income Medicare Beneficiary program) from 120% to 200% of the poverty line.
Has the federal government pay 100% of Medicaid costs for people newly covered by the expansions, rather than splitting costs with states.

Gives beneficiaries three months of retroactive coverage when they apply, lets states keep people enrolled for 12 months at a time, and stops counting in-kind support, life insurance, vehicles, burial funds, and pensions toward resource limits.
Bars providers from refusing service or billing these low-income beneficiaries for Medicare cost-sharing, and makes Medicare cost-sharing assistance non-countable income for other benefit programs.
Transfers $50 million per year from the Medicare trust funds to state health insurance assistance programs to do outreach to seniors who qualify for help but are not enrolled.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through a 100% federal match for the expanded Medicaid coverage and $250 million over five years transferred from the Medicare trust funds.

drawbacks.text: The bill adds open-ended federal entitlement spending with no offset, and draws $50 million a year from the Medicare Hospital Insurance and Supplementary Medical Insurance trust funds for outreach grants.

It repeals the Qualifying Individual program, which currently provides premium assistance to people between 120% and 135% of the poverty line, requiring those beneficiaries to shift into the newly expanded program.
It imposes new federal eligibility and enrollment rules on state Medicaid programs, which must change their systems even though states face no new cost for the expansion itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is targeted and real: low-income seniors between the poverty line and twice the poverty line face Medicare premiums and cost-sharing they often cannot afford, and research consistently shows many who qualify for existing help never enroll — which is why the bill pairs the expansion with outreach money. The cost is genuine new federal spending without offsets, but it is modest relative to Medicare's overall budget, and paying 100% of the expansion shields states from new costs. The main design weakness is the open-ended commitment with no dedicated funding source.

outcome.mechanism: The Energy and Commerce Committee approved it by voice vote and it was placed on the House calendar in January 2020, but House leadership never brought it up for a vote, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Kim introduced the bill on October 15, 2019, after the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee had held hearings on the topic in September.
It was referred to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee.
The Energy and Commerce Committee ordered it reported by voice vote on October 17, 2019, and formally reported it with a written report on January 24, 2020.
The Ways and Means Committee was discharged the same day, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar — the list of bills awaiting a House floor vote.
No further action was taken, and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, without a House or Senate vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low-income Medicare beneficiaries gained nothing and kept paying premiums and copays out of pocket. The federal budget avoided new entitlement spending, and no provider or state lost anything it currently receives.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; seniors kept paying out of pocket

for.name: Rep. Andy Kim
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 15, 2019 and gave introductory remarks.

for.name: 7 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Blunt Rochester, Evans, Cuellar, Matsui, Pascrell, Malinowski, and Norcross).

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (Chair Frank Pallone)
for.what_they_did: Held subcommittee hearings, marked the bill up, and reported it by voice vote on October 17, 2019; formally reported it January 24, 2020.

against.name: Speaker Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote after it was placed on the Union Calendar in January 2020.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all seven cosponsors were Democrats and no Republicans signed on, but the committee reported the bill by voice vote with no recorded partisan split, and no floor vote ever tested where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Hospitals and providers serving low-income Medicare beneficiaries
industries.note: The bill would route new federal money through Medicaid to pay providers for Medicare cost-sharing on behalf of newly eligible beneficiaries, and states would have to let non-contracted providers bill for it. Providers gain revenue; beneficiaries gain coverage of the same charges.

industries.industry: State Medicaid programs and state governments
industries.note: A 100% federal matching rate means Washington pays the entire cost of the expanded eligibility, and states receive new federal grants for senior counseling and outreach programs.

industries.industry: Part D drug plans and insurers
industries.note: Looser resource tests and simpler enrollment would make more low-income seniors eligible for the Part D low-income subsidy, bringing plans additional federally subsidized enrollees while subjecting them to more subsidy administration.
